strengths: Addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: measuring social-bias changes after continued masked-language-model training. Comparing retrained models with their pretrained bases is a useful experimental framing.

Evaluates four MLM checkpoints, two established benchmarks, several existing measures, and both stereotypical and anti-stereotypical retraining. Extensive category-level results make the observed patterns inspectable.
CRR, ΔP, and ΔPA recover the intended retraining direction in all 72 aggregate cases. This provides useful evidence of sensitivity to the particular intervention tested.
weaknesses: The central claim of superior bias-measurement accuracy exceeds the validation provided. Retraining and evaluation reuse CrowS-Pairs, without separately reported results on an independent bias test set. Moreover, the training corpus's stereotype direction is assumed to establish the correct bias change for every category. This evaluation can reward memorization and improved token prediction. Held-out examples and neutral or balanced retraining controls are needed to distinguish these effects from accurate social-bias measurement.

Human-annotation alignment is weak. In Appendix M, the best proposed AUROC is 0.572 versus AUL's 0.566 for RoBERTa, and 0.571 versus 0.569 for BERT. These near-chance results, with only 58 negative pairs and no confidence intervals or significance comparisons, provide little support for superiority. Furthermore, annotations identify stereotypes in text rather than independently measuring model bias.

Equation 10 mishandles ties: comparing an unchanged model with itself produces BSRT = 0 because every strict inequality is false. Section 3.5.2 would interpret this as a directional bias shift, although nothing changed. This is particularly relevant to discrete rank-based measures. Tie handling and a no-change control are necessary before interpreting the score around its proposed neutral value of 50.

The statistical analysis does not establish the claimed comparative reliability. Appendix P's McNemar test examines changes in binary sentence preferences, whereas BSRT examines changes in preference margins; these are different quantities. Neither additional significant results nor more extreme scores establish greater accuracy. Repeated retraining runs and uncertainty estimates are absent. Table 3 also reports 0.028 for a model with one erroneous category among nine, suggesting an incorrect or unexplained denominator.

Reproducibility is insufficient despite specifying checkpoints, masking probability, epochs, and an 80/20 split. Learning rate, optimizer, batch size, random seeds, exact splits, and precise attention aggregation are missing. The claimed released package has no identifiable link or version in the manuscript. Equations 11–12 also sum over all sentence tokens despite the descriptions of subset-based baseline scoring, leaving implementation fidelity unclear.

The distinctive benefit of attention weighting is not demonstrated. Previously introduced CRR and unweighted ΔP already attain the reported 100% directional accuracy, while CRRA performs slightly worse. CRRA changes both the rank transformation and attention weighting, so their effects are not isolated. This limits the supported methodological contribution, independently of the soundness concerns above.

The interpretation of social bias needs greater care. Anti-stereotypical sentences are repeatedly equated with bias against advantaged groups, although the StereoSet example in Table 12 changes an attribute of the same group. Likewise, disagreements between metrics are described as underestimation or overestimation without an established reference value. These construct-validity and evidential gaps prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current version.
